tool.name: TypeScript
tool.tagline: JavaScript with a static type system that catches bugs before they run
tool.description: TypeScript is a typed superset of JavaScript: it adds type annotations, interfaces, generics and a powerful type checker, then compiles to plain JavaScript that runs anywhere. It is the default choice for large front-end and Node.js codebases because it catches mistakes early, powers editor autocomplete and refactoring, and documents APIs in the code itself.

glossary.def: The TypeScript compiler's command. It checks your TypeScript code for type mistakes and can write out the plain JavaScript version.
The settings file at the root of a TypeScript project. It tells tsc which files belong to the project, which checks to run and what to write out.
One setting in the compilerOptions section of tsconfig.json, such as strict or target, that changes what tsc checks or writes out.
In TypeScript, to write out the output files - the JavaScript, and optionally type description files - that tsc produces from your code.
TypeScript's rule that all type information is deleted when the code is turned into JavaScript, so types cost nothing - and check nothing - while the program runs.
Running TypeScript by simply deleting its type annotations without checking them. Fast tools such as esbuild and recent Node.js versions work this way.
Deciding whether two types fit together by comparing their shapes - which properties they have and of what types - rather than their names.
Deciding whether types fit together by name: a value fits only if it was declared as that exact type. TypeScript is mostly structural, but a few features behave nominally.
One of JavaScript's simple, one-piece kinds of value: string, number, boolean, bigint, symbol, null and undefined. Every other value is an object.
In TypeScript, the compiler working out a type by itself from the code - let n = 0 makes n a number without you writing it.
TypeScript giving a function's parameters their types from where the function is used: in [1, 2].map(n => n * 2), n is known to be a number because the array holds numbers.
A type that allows exactly one value, such as "left" or 42. Combined with |, literal types list every allowed value.
TypeScript turning an exact type like "dark" into the general type string. It happens for let variables and object properties, because their values could change later.
Writing value as SomeType to make TypeScript treat a value as that type. It skips most checking and changes nothing while the program runs.
A ! after a value (value!) telling TypeScript to assume it isn't null or undefined. Nothing is checked while the program runs.
The outline of a function: its parameters with their types and its return type, without the body.
A type describing a function's parameters and return value, written like (name: string) => number.
A type that lists an object's properties and their types, like { id: number; name: string }.
An object written out directly in code with curly braces, like { id: 1, name: "Ada" }.
An extra check on an object written directly where a type is expected: properties the type doesn't list are reported, because they're usually typos.
A rule for objects used as lookup tables: { [key: string]: number } means any string key is allowed and every value is a number.
A type that allows a value of any one of several types, written with |, like string | number.
A name for any type, created with the type keyword, such as type Id = string | number.
TypeScript working out a more specific type for a variable after a check: inside if (typeof x === "string"), a string | number is just a string.
Any check that TypeScript uses to narrow a type, such as typeof, instanceof, in, or a function you write that returns x is T.
A check that code handles every member of a union, so adding a new member makes the compiler point at every place you forgot to update.
A type written A & B: a value must have everything from both A and B.
A function return type written x is T. When the function returns true, TypeScript narrows x to T where the function was called.
A function whose return type is asserts x is T. It throws if the check fails, so after the call TypeScript treats x as T.
A union of object types that share one property, the tag, whose exact value differs per member, so checking the tag tells TypeScript which member you have.
The shared tag property of a discriminated union, such as kind or status, whose exact value identifies each member.
A ready-made generic type built into TypeScript that turns one type into another, such as Partial<T>, Pick<T, K> or Record<K, V>.
The actual type filled in for a type parameter, like string in Array<string>.
A limit on a type parameter, written T extends X: T can be any type, as long as it fits X.
A TypeScript file ending in .d.ts that holds only types - what exists and its shape - and no runnable code. It describes JavaScript code to TypeScript.
A community project that publishes type descriptions for JavaScript packages that don't ship their own, installed as @types/<name> packages.
A JavaScript file that uses the standard import and export keywords - the module system built into the language, as opposed to Node.js's older CommonJS.
How TypeScript (or Node.js, or a bundler) works out which file or package an import refers to.
TypeScript combining several declarations with the same name - for example two interfaces called Box - into one.
Adding properties to types declared by another module or package, or with declare global to built-in global types, using declaration merging.
A type that builds an object type by going through a list of keys, { [K in Keys]: ... }, and choosing each property's type.
A mapped type that loops over keyof T. It keeps T's optional and readonly markers, and turns arrays into arrays rather than into objects.
A type that picks one of two types based on a test: T extends U ? X : Y reads 'if T fits U, then X, otherwise Y'.
A conditional type applied to each member of a union separately, with the results joined back into a union.
A type looked up from another type by key: User["email"] is the type of User's email property.
A string type written with backticks, like `${number}px`, that describes every string matching that pattern.
One of several declared ways to call the same function, each with its own parameter and return types. The last, hidden one - the implementation signature - has the body.
Whether a value of one type may be used where another type is expected. If S is assignable to T, you can pass an S wherever a T is wanted.
How a generic type's compatibility follows its type parameter: covariant (a Box of Dog fits a Box of Animal), contravariant (the reverse) or invariant (only the exact same type fits).
Writing as const after a value so TypeScript infers the most exact type: literal types, readonly properties and readonly tuples.
A type like string & { __brand: "UserId" }: a plain string while running, but kept apart from other strings by TypeScript, so different kinds of IDs can't be mixed up.
A type every value fits into - in TypeScript, unknown. A bottom type is the opposite: no value fits it (never).
An object type whose properties are all optional. TypeScript requires a value assigned to it to share at least one property, to catch typos.
A tsconfig.json feature that splits a large codebase into smaller TypeScript projects that depend on each other and can be built separately and only when changed.
One computation of a generic type with concrete types filled in. The checker counts them; huge counts mean expensive types.
The TypeScript package used as a library: your own programs can read, inspect and type-check code the same way tsc does.
In TypeScript, the strict setting in tsconfig.json, which switches on the whole family of stricter type checks. (JavaScript's "use strict" mode is a different thing.)
The TypeScript check (part of strict) that keeps null and undefined out of other types, so a value that may be missing must say so, like string | undefined.
The TypeScript check (part of strict) that reports parameters and variables whose type would silently become any because nothing says what they are.
To rewrite newer JavaScript features into older, equivalent code, so the program runs on older browsers or engines.
Extra code that adds a missing built-in feature, like a newer array method, to older browsers or engines so code that uses it still works.
The package manager that comes with Node.js. It downloads JavaScript packages into your project's node_modules folder; npx runs a command from an installed package.
A file that links compiled code back to the lines of your original code, so error messages and debuggers show what you actually wrote.
The standard linter setup for TypeScript: a collection of ESLint rules that understand types, such as spotting promises you forgot to await.
Recursion where the recursive call is the very last thing done, so nothing is left to finish afterwards. Compilers can turn it into a plain loop.
A tuple type with a spread inside, like [...A, ...B] or [string, ...number[]], so its length isn't fixed by the type.
A script that rewrites lots of code automatically, for example updating every call to a renamed function.

concepts.name: Why TypeScript
concepts.summary: TypeScript is JavaScript plus type labels that are checked before the code runs, then deleted so plain JavaScript runs.
concepts.why: Knowing what TypeScript checks, and what it can't check once the program is running, shapes every decision you make with it.
concepts.body:
JavaScript is **dynamically typed**: a variable can hold a number now and a string later, and nothing checks whether that makes sense until the line actually runs.

**TypeScript** is JavaScript with one addition: you can write down what type each value should have. Such a label is a **type annotation** — `let age: number = 36` says `age` must always hold a number. All JavaScript is already valid TypeScript.

A program called the **type checker** compares every use of a value with what its annotation allows. It reports mistakes, such as a misspelled property or a string passed where a number belongs, while you're still writing. Languages that check types ahead of time like this are called **statically typed**.

Browsers and Node.js only run JavaScript, so TypeScript has to be turned into JavaScript first. Translating code into another form before it runs is called **compiling**, done by a **compiler**. TypeScript's compiler, `tsc`, does both jobs: it checks the types, then writes out plain JavaScript.

The key idea: types are **erased**. When the compiler writes the JavaScript, it simply deletes every annotation. So while the program is running — at **runtime** — no type information exists: nothing checks arguments, and nothing gets slower. Data from outside, say from `JSON.parse` or `fetch`, has whatever type you *told* TypeScript it has; nothing verifies it.

What you get in exchange:

- **Errors caught early**: typos in property names, using something that might be `undefined`, passing text where a number is expected.
- **A smarter code editor**: in an editor such as VS Code, **autocomplete** (suggestions as you type) and safe renaming use the types.
- **Documentation that can't go stale**: a function's types say exactly what it accepts and returns.
- **Safer changes**: change a type and the compiler lists every place that needs updating.

TypeScript's checking is **structural**: two types fit together if their shapes match — the same properties with the same types — whatever they are called.

You can adopt it gradually: rename a `.js` file to `.ts`, fix the errors it reports, and tighten the checks over time. Errors found at **compile time** (while the compiler works) don't stop the JavaScript being written by default; some tools skip checking entirely (next lesson).
takeaways: TypeScript = JavaScript + type annotations, checked before the code runs
Types are erased: no checks and no cost at runtime
Typing is structural: matching shapes count, not matching names
pitfalls: Assuming TypeScript checks outside data (a server's reply, parsed JSON) while the program runs — it does not.

quiz.q: You annotate a parameter as number and a caller passes a value parsed from JSON that is actually a string. What happens at runtime?
options: TypeScript throws a TypeError at the call
The string is converted to a number automatically
Nothing special: the string flows through, because types are erased
quiz.explain: Type annotations disappear after compilation, so TypeScript cannot validate data whose type it was merely told.

quiz.q: Two types with different names describe exactly the same properties. Can a value of one be used where the other is expected?
options: Yes, compatibility is based on shape
Only if one is declared to extend the other
quiz.explain: TypeScript's checking is structural, so types with identical shapes are interchangeable.

concepts.name: tsc and tsconfig.json
concepts.summary: Install the TypeScript compiler, run it on a project, and set it up with a tsconfig.json file.
concepts.why: Every TypeScript project is driven by a tsconfig.json file; knowing its main settings saves hours of confusing errors.
concepts.body:
TypeScript itself is a **package**: ready-made code, published with a name and version, that you install into a project. JavaScript packages are installed with **npm**, the installer that comes with Node.js. In a terminal, inside your project folder, run `npm install --save-dev typescript` (`--save-dev` notes it's only needed while developing). Then run the compiler with `npx tsc`.

`npx tsc --init` writes a starter **tsconfig.json**: the settings file that marks the root of a project and tells `tsc` which files to compile and how. Its `compilerOptions` section holds the settings. The ones you'll touch most:

- `include` / `exclude`: which of your code files belong to the project, e.g. `["src"]`.
- `target`: which yearly edition of JavaScript to write out (`ES2022`, `ESNext`...). For an older edition, newer language features are rewritten into older equivalents.
- `outDir` / `rootDir`: where the compiled `.js` files go, and which of your folders is mirrored into it.
- `strict`: turns on the whole family of strict checks. Always enable it in new projects.

- `lib`: which built-in features the checker should assume exist: `ES2023` for the language's own, `DOM` for the browser's. It only affects checking. It doesn't add missing features to old browsers; code that does that is called a **polyfill**.
- `module` / `moduleResolution`: how imports are written and found. Use `"nodenext"` for code Node.js runs directly, or `"preserve"` with `"bundler"` when a bundler such as Vite, esbuild or webpack packs your code.
- `noEmit`: check only; don't **emit** (write out) any files.

Useful commands: `tsc` (build the project in the current folder), `tsc --noEmit` (check types only), `tsc --watch` (rebuild whenever a file changes), and `tsc -p path/to/tsconfig.json` (use a specific settings file).

Many tools never use `tsc` to produce JavaScript. esbuild, swc, Vite, Bun, Deno and recent Node.js versions just delete the types without checking them — **type stripping**. That's fast, but type errors then only show up in your editor or when you run `tsc --noEmit`.

So add `tsc --noEmit` to your project's automatic checks. Teams usually run those in **CI**: a service that builds and tests every change before it's accepted into the shared code.

One gotcha: running `tsc file.ts` with a file name *ignores* tsconfig.json entirely and uses default settings, which surprises almost everyone once.
takeaways: `npx tsc --init` creates tsconfig.json; `npx tsc` builds the project it describes
`strict: true` in every new project
Type-stripping tools don't check types: run `tsc --noEmit` in CI
`lib` only tells the checker which built-in features exist; it adds no polyfills
pitfalls: Running `tsc somefile.ts` and wondering why your tsconfig settings are ignored.

quiz.q: Your project builds with esbuild, which strips types. Where will type errors be reported?
options: esbuild fails the build on any type error
Only by tsc (e.g. tsc --noEmit) or the editor
quiz.explain: Type-stripping tools skip checking entirely, so tsc --noEmit is needed to catch type errors.

quiz.q: You set target to ES5 and call the array method includes, which very old browsers lack. What does tsc do about it?
options: Nothing; lib only tells the checker which built-in features exist
quiz.explain: tsc rewrites newer language features for old targets but never adds missing built-in methods; lib only tells the checker what exists.

concepts.name: Primitive and basic types
concepts.summary: The everyday types: string, number, boolean, null, undefined and a few rarer ones, and how to label a variable with one.
concepts.why: These are the building blocks every other type is made from.
concepts.body:
TypeScript uses the names of JavaScript's simple, one-piece values — the **primitive types** — written in lowercase:

- `string`, `number` (all numbers, whole and decimal alike), `boolean`
- `bigint` for whole numbers too big for `number` (`10n`), and `symbol` for unique labels
- `null` and `undefined`, each a type with exactly one value

Write them in lowercase. `String`, `Number` and `Boolean` with a capital letter name rarely used object versions of these values (`new String("x")`) and are almost never what you want.

You annotate a variable with a colon after its name: `let count: number = 0`. From then on the checker enforces it: `count = "ten"` is an error, and so is calling `count.toUpperCase()`. The checker knows which methods and properties each type has, so the editor can autocomplete `name.` with string methods.

Arrays are written `number[]` (or `Array<number>`), and an object's shape is described by its properties: `{ id: number; title: string }`. Both get their own lessons.

There are a few special types you will meet early:

- `any` switches checking off for a value. Avoid it (more later).
- `void` is the "return type" of a function that returns nothing useful.
- `object` means "any value that isn't one of the primitives"; it's rarely precise enough to be useful.

With the `strict` setting on (every new project should turn it on), `null` and `undefined` don't sneak into other types: a `string` variable can never hold `null` unless you allow it with `string | null` (the `|` means "or"). This one rule removes the most common runtime error in JavaScript: reading a property of `undefined`.
takeaways: Use lowercase `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `bigint`, `symbol`
`number` covers whole and decimal numbers alike
With `strict` on, `null`/`undefined` must be allowed explicitly
pitfalls: Writing `String` or `Number` (the rarely used object versions) instead of `string` / `number`.

quiz.q: With strict on, which declaration accepts the value null?
quiz.explain: With strict on, null is a type of its own, so it must be allowed explicitly with | null.

quiz.q: What is the type of both 3 and 3.14 in TypeScript?
quiz.explain: JavaScript has one numeric type for both, so TypeScript has one: number (plus bigint for big integers).

concepts.name: Type annotations and inference
concepts.summary: Where you write types yourself and where TypeScript works them out for you, and why let and const can get different types.
concepts.why: Good TypeScript labels the edges of your code and lets TypeScript work out the rest, which keeps code short and still safe.
concepts.body:
You rarely need to label everything. TypeScript **infers** a type from the starting value: `let count = 0` makes `count` a `number`, and `const names = ["a", "b"]` is `string[]`. Hover over a name in your editor to see what was inferred.

Where annotations earn their keep:

- **Function parameters**: their types can't be worked out from the body. Without the `noImplicitAny` check (part of `strict`) they silently become `any`, which switches checking off.
- **Return types of exported functions**, so a change in the body can't silently change what other files rely on.
- **Variables declared without a value** (`let result: string;`) and **empty arrays** (`const ids: number[] = []`).
- When you want a *wider* or *narrower* type than the one inferred.

Inference also flows "backwards". In `names.map(n => n.length)`, the callback parameter `n` is a `string` because `map` knows what the array holds. This is called **contextual typing**.

Watch out for **literal widening**. A `const` can never change, so `const mode = "dark"` gets the exact type `"dark"` — a **literal type**, which allows only that one value.

A `let` can be reassigned, so `let mode = "dark"` widens to `string`. Object properties can change too, so `{ mode: "dark" }` has `mode: string`. This matters when a function only accepts `"dark"` or `"light"`; later lessons show `as const` and `satisfies` for those cases.

An annotation (`const x: T = value`) asks the checker to verify that the value fits `T`. A **type assertion** (`value as T`) instead *tells* the checker to trust you, and skips most checking. Prefer annotations; reach for `as` only when you know something the compiler can't.
takeaways: Annotate parameters, exported return types and empty values; let inference do the rest
`const` keeps literal types; `let` and object properties widen them
Annotation = checked; `value as T` = trusted, not checked
pitfalls: Using `as` to silence an error rather than fixing the type — it hides real bugs.

quiz.q: What is the inferred type of p in: let p = "north"?
quiz.explain: let bindings can be reassigned, so the literal type widens to string.

quiz.q: In [1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 2), why does n need no annotation?
options: Because n is declared with const
Because map's type says the callback receives the array's elements (contextual typing)
quiz.explain: The callback's position supplies the expected type, so n is inferred as number.

concepts.name: Arrays and tuples
concepts.summary: Type lists with T[], fixed-length data with tuples, and prevent changes with readonly arrays.
concepts.why: Lists are everywhere, and tuples are how TypeScript types small fixed groups of values, such as a function that returns two things at once.
concepts.body:
An **array type** is written `T[]` or `Array<T>`, where `T` stands for the element type; both forms mean the same. For an array that mixes types, put the choices in parentheses with `|` ("or"): `(string | number)[]`. Array methods are fully typed, so `nums.map(n => n.toFixed(1))` returns `string[]`.

A **tuple** is an array with a fixed length and a known type at each position: `[string, number]`. Tuples suit small results where position carries the meaning: a key-value pair, a coordinate, or a function returning two things:

```typescript
function useCounter(): [number, () => void] { /* ... */ }
const [count, increment] = useCounter();
```

Tuple positions can have **labels** for documentation (`[x: number, y: number]`), be **optional** (`[string, number?]`) or collect the **rest** (`[string, ...number[]]`).

Note that an array you write out directly is inferred as an array, not a tuple: `const p = [1, "a"]` is `(string | number)[]`. Annotate the tuple type, or use `as const` (covered later) to get one.

**`readonly`** arrays (`readonly string[]` or `ReadonlyArray<string>`) remove the methods that change an array, like `push` and `sort`. Use them for parameters you don't intend to change; callers can still pass ordinary arrays. The reverse is not allowed: a readonly array can't be passed where a changeable one is expected.

One important hole: by default, reading `arr[10]` is typed as the element type even if the array is shorter, so the result could really be `undefined`. The `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` setting (see the strict-options lesson) makes such reads `T | undefined`.
takeaways: `T[]` and `Array<T>` are the same type
Tuples type fixed-length positional data: `[string, number]`
Take `readonly T[]` parameters when you don't mutate the input
pitfalls: Expecting `const pair = [1, "a"]` to be a tuple — it's inferred as `(string | number)[]`.

quiz.q: What type is inferred for const pair = ["x", 1]?
quiz.explain: Array literals are inferred as arrays of the union of element types unless annotated or asserted with as const.

quiz.q: Can you pass a readonly number[] to a function whose parameter is number[]?
options: No, because the function could mutate it
Yes, readonly is ignored in parameters
Only if the array is empty
quiz.explain: number[] promises push/sort are available, which a readonly array cannot provide, so the assignment is rejected.

concepts.name: Typing functions
concepts.summary: Annotate parameters and return types, use optional, default and rest parameters, and write function types for callbacks.
concepts.why: Functions are the main boundaries in any program, and their signatures (parameter and return types) are where TypeScript catches most mistakes.
concepts.body:
Annotate each **parameter**; the **return type** is inferred but worth stating on exported functions:

```typescript
function formatPrice(amount: number, currency: string = "EUR"): string { ... }
```

Parameter options:

- **Optional**: `name?: string` — the parameter may be omitted and has type `string | undefined` inside.
- **Default**: `currency = "EUR"` — also optional for callers, and the type is inferred from the default.
- **Rest**: `...values: number[]` collects remaining arguments into an array.

TypeScript checks calls strictly: too few or too many arguments is an error, unlike plain JavaScript.

A **function type** describes a callback or a function-valued variable: `(item: string, index: number) => boolean`. The parameter *names* are only documentation; the types and positions matter. A callback with *fewer* parameters is fine where more are offered — that's why `arr.forEach(x => ...)` works even though `forEach` passes three arguments.

Return types worth knowing:

- `void` — the function returns nothing meaningful. A callback type returning `void` may be given a function that returns something; the value is just ignored.
- `never` — the function never returns normally (it always throws or loops forever).

Arrow functions and function expressions are typed the same way. When a function is passed directly as an argument, its parameters get their types from that spot (contextual typing), so you usually don't annotate them there.

The `this` parameter is a fake first parameter (`function (this: HTMLElement) {}`) that declares what `this` must be; it is erased from the JavaScript output.
takeaways: Always annotate parameters; state return types on exported functions
`p?: T` is optional (`T | undefined` inside); defaults make parameters optional too
Function types look like `(a: A, b: B) => R`
`void` = no useful return value; `never` = never returns
pitfalls: Writing `(string) => void` — that declares a parameter *named* string of type any.

quiz.q: A callback type is (value: string, index: number) => void. Is the function (v: string) => v.length assignable to it?
options: No, it returns a number instead of void
Yes: fewer parameters are allowed and a void return type ignores the returned value
quiz.explain: Functions with fewer parameters are compatible, and a void-returning function type accepts functions that return a value.

quiz.q: Inside function f(label?: string), what is the type of label?
quiz.explain: An optional parameter may be omitted, so its type includes undefined.

concepts.name: Object types and interfaces
concepts.summary: Describe the shape of an object inline or with an interface, including optional properties, methods and extending.
concepts.why: Almost all real data is objects; interfaces are how a codebase names their shapes and shares them.
concepts.body:
An **object type** lists properties and their types: `{ id: number; name: string }`. Separators can be `;` or `,`. When a shape is used in more than one place, give it a name with an **interface**:

```typescript
interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email?: string;              // optional
  greet(other: User): string;  // method
}
```

Any object with at least those properties fits `User`. No class or special declaration is needed, because TypeScript's typing is structural. Extra properties are fine when you pass an existing variable.

There is one exception you will hit quickly. An **object literal** — an object written out with `{ }` — placed directly where a type is expected gets an **excess property check**. `const u: User = { id: 1, name: "A", emial: "x" }` is an error, because a property the type doesn't know about is most likely a typo.

Interfaces can **extend** others, combining shapes:

```typescript
interface Admin extends User { permissions: string[] }
```

Reading a property that isn't declared is an error, which catches typos. Sometimes an object is a lookup table whose keys you don't know in advance. For that, write an **index signature**: `{ [key: string]: number }` means any string key, each with a number value. The built-in `Record<string, number>` says the same (covered later).

Optional properties are typed `T | undefined` when you read them, so you must check before using one: `user.email?.toLowerCase()`.

Object types and interfaces also describe functions' parameters and return values, nested objects and arrays of objects, so you'll write them constantly. Give a name to shapes that several files share; write one-off shapes inline.
takeaways: Interfaces name the shape of an object; any object with those members fits
`prop?: T` marks optional properties (read as `T | undefined`)
Object literals get excess property checks that catch typos
`extends` builds bigger interfaces from smaller ones
pitfalls: Assuming excess property checks always apply — they only apply to object literals written directly where the type is expected.

quiz.q: const p = { x: 1, y: 2, label: "a" }; const q: { x: number; y: number } = p; Is this an error?
options: No: excess property checks only apply to object literals written directly at the assignment
Yes, label is an excess property
Yes, the types have different names
quiz.explain: p is not a fresh literal, so its extra property is allowed by structural typing.

quiz.q: How do you declare that a User may or may not have a phone property?
quiz.explain: A question mark after the property name marks it optional.

concepts.name: Union and literal types
concepts.summary: Combine types with | and restrict values to exact strings or numbers with literal types.
concepts.why: Unions of exact values replace error-prone free-form strings and model the 'one of these' choices that appear in every program.
concepts.body:
A **union type** `A | B` means a value can be either. `string | number` accepts both; `User | null` is how you model "maybe there's a user".

A literal type is a single exact value — a **literal**, written directly in the code — used as a type: `"left"`, `42`, `true`. On their own they're odd, but unions of them are one of TypeScript's best features:

```typescript
type Align = "left" | "center" | "right";
function align(text: string, how: Align) { ... }
align("hi", "centre"); // error: not assignable to Align
```

Your editor autocompletes the allowed values, and the compiler reports typos, at zero runtime cost: the values stay ordinary strings. The same works for numbers (`type Dice = 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6`), and `boolean` is simply `true | false`.

What can you do with a union value? Only what's valid for *every* member. With `id: string | number` you can call `id.toString()` (both have it) but not `id.toUpperCase()`. To use member-specific operations, you **narrow** the union first, usually with a check like `typeof id === "string"`. That's the next lesson.

The `type` keyword creates a **type alias**: a name for any type, including unions. (An `interface` can only name the shape of an object.)

Remember literal widening: `let how = "left"` is a `string`, so passing it where `Align` is expected fails. Either annotate (`let how: Align = "left"`) or use `const`.

Unions also work inside arrays: `(string | number)[]` is an array whose elements can each be either, while `string[] | number[]` is either an all-string or an all-number array.
takeaways: `A | B` = a value of either type
Unions of exact strings replace free-form strings, at zero runtime cost
On a union you can only use what every member supports — narrow first
pitfalls: Losing a literal type through `let` and then failing to pass it to a function expecting the union.

quiz.q: Given x: string | number, which expression compiles without narrowing?
quiz.explain: Only members shared by both string and number are allowed on the union, and both have toString.

quiz.q: What is the difference between (string | number)[] and string[] | number[]?
options: The first allows mixed arrays; the second is all-strings or all-numbers
quiz.explain: The parentheses put the union on each element, while the second form is a union of two array types.

concepts.name: null, undefined and strictNullChecks
concepts.summary: Model missing values explicitly with T | undefined, and handle them with checks, ?. and ??.
concepts.why: Reading a property of undefined is JavaScript's most common crash; strict null checking catches it before the code runs.
concepts.body:
With `strictNullChecks` (part of `strict`), `null` and `undefined` are types of their own. A `string` is always a string; something that may be missing must say so: `string | undefined` or `User | null`.

Many built-in functions return values that may be missing, and TypeScript types them that way: `array.find(...)` returns `T | undefined`, `map.get(key)` returns `V | undefined`, and `document.querySelector(...)` returns `Element | null`. The compiler won't let you use the result as if it were definitely there.

Ways to deal with it:

- **Check first**: `if (user) { user.name }` or `if (user !== undefined)`. Inside the block the type is narrowed to `User`.
- **Optional chaining**: `user?.address?.city` stops and gives `undefined` if something is missing.
- **Nullish coalescing**: `user?.name ?? "anonymous"` supplies a default for `null`/`undefined` only (unlike `||`, which also replaces `""` and `0`).
- **Early return**: `if (!user) return;` narrows the rest of the function.

There is also the **non-null assertion**, `value!`, which tells the compiler "trust me, this isn't null". It disappears from the JavaScript and checks nothing while the program runs.

So a wrong `!` becomes exactly the crash strict checking was meant to prevent. Use it only when you truly know better, and prefer a check that throws a clear error.

Convention: many codebases use `undefined` for "absent" (it's what optional properties and failed lookups produce) and keep `null` for values that functions deliberately return as null, like `querySelector`. Be consistent within a codebase.
takeaways: With `strict` on, possibly-missing values are typed `T | undefined` or `T | null`
Narrow with checks or early returns; use `?.` and `??` for short access
`??` only replaces null/undefined; `||` also replaces 0 and ""
pitfalls: Sprinkling `!` non-null assertions to silence errors — they check nothing while the program runs.

quiz.q: What is the type of [1, 2, 3].find(n => n > 2) under strict mode?
quiz.explain: find returns undefined when nothing matches, and its signature says so.

quiz.q: count is typed number | undefined and is 0. What does count ?? 10 evaluate to?
quiz.explain: ?? only falls back on null or undefined, so 0 is kept.

concepts.name: Type narrowing
concepts.summary: How TypeScript refines a union to a specific member using typeof, equality, in, instanceof and control flow.
concepts.why: Narrowing is how you work with unions safely; it's the everyday skill that makes TypeScript feel natural.
concepts.body:
**Narrowing** is the checker following your code's path through `if`, `return` and `switch`, and making a variable's type more specific after each check. Inside `if (typeof x === "string") { ... }` a `string | number` is just `string`.

The checks TypeScript understands:

- **`typeof`**: `"string"`, `"number"`, `"boolean"`, `"bigint"`, `"symbol"`, `"undefined"`, `"function"`, `"object"`. Beware: `typeof null === "object"`, and TypeScript knows that — a `typeof x === "object"` check leaves `null` in the type.
- **Truthiness**: `if (value)` removes `null` and `undefined` (and also falsy members like `""` and `0` — be careful with numbers and strings).
- **Equality**: `x === "left"`, `x !== null`, and `switch` on a union of literal types.
- **`in`**: `"swim" in animal` keeps the members that have (or may have) a `swim` property.
- **`instanceof`**: `err instanceof Error` narrows to the class type.
- **`Array.isArray(x)`** narrows to the array member.

Narrowing works with early exits too: after `if (typeof x === "string") return;`, the rest of the function knows `x` is a number. Assignments narrow as well — after `x = 5` the checker knows `x` is a number until it changes again.

The checker narrows **variables and parameters**, not arbitrary expressions. Narrowing of a property like `obj.value` is lost after a function call that might have changed it, and narrowing inside callbacks may be reset for `let` variables because the callback could run later. Copying to a `const` first (`const v = obj.value`) usually fixes such cases.

When these checks can't express what you need, you can write your own checking functions — a later lesson.
takeaways: Checks like `typeof`, `===`, `in`, `instanceof` narrow unions automatically
Early returns narrow the rest of the function
`typeof x === "object"` does not exclude null
pitfalls: Using a truthiness check on `number | undefined` and accidentally treating 0 as missing.

quiz.q: x is string[] | string | null. After if (typeof x === "object") { ... }, what is x inside the block?
quiz.explain: typeof null is "object", so null stays in the narrowed type alongside the array.

quiz.q: Which check narrows err (typed unknown) so that err.message is allowed?
quiz.explain: instanceof Error narrows to Error, which declares message.

concepts.name: any, unknown and never
concepts.summary: Why any switches checking off, why unknown is the safe 'could be anything' type, and where never appears.
concepts.why: Choosing unknown over any is one of the biggest differences between safe and leaky TypeScript.
concepts.body:
**`any`** opts a value out of type checking. You can call anything on it and assign it anywhere, and the compiler stays silent. Worse, `any` *spreads*: `const n = anyValue.count` is also `any`, and so on through your program. It exists for moving old JavaScript over and for rare emergencies; `noImplicitAny` (part of `strict`) at least stops the compiler inventing it for parameters you didn't annotate.

**`unknown`** is the safe "could be anything" type. Every value can be assigned *to* `unknown`, but you can't do anything *with* an `unknown` until you narrow it:

```typescript
function handle(data: unknown) {
  data.toUpperCase();                 // error
  if (typeof data === "string") data.toUpperCase(); // ok
}
```

Use `unknown` for data whose shape you haven't checked yet: parsed JSON, messages from other windows, and errors caught in `catch` (with `strict`, `catch (e)` gives `e: unknown`).

Check such data by hand, as in the code below, or with a **library** — ready-made code you install as a package — built for checking data, such as Zod. Either way, the narrowed result is properly typed.

**`never`** is the empty type: no value has it. It shows up as:

- the return type of functions that always throw,
- what's left after narrowing has ruled out every possibility,
- the result of impossible demands, such as a value that must be a string and a number at once.

That second use powers **exhaustiveness checks**. In the `default` branch of a `switch` over a union, assign the value to a `never` variable. If someone later adds a new member to the union, that line stops compiling and points you to the switch you forgot to update.

Rule of thumb: never write `any` when `unknown` would do.
takeaways: `any` disables checking and spreads; avoid it
`unknown` accepts anything but must be narrowed before use
`never` = no possible value; use it for exhaustiveness checks
pitfalls: Typing parsed JSON as `any` and letting unchecked data flow through the program.

quiz.q: data is typed unknown. Which line compiles?
quiz.explain: Anything can be assigned to unknown, but you cannot use it or assign it to a specific type without narrowing.

quiz.q: In the default branch of an exhaustive switch over a union, what type does the narrowed variable have?
quiz.explain: Every member was handled by earlier cases, so nothing remains and the type is never.

concepts.name: Type aliases vs interfaces
concepts.summary: When to use type and when to use interface, and how extends compares with combining types using &.
concepts.why: Teams argue about this constantly; knowing the real differences lets you pick quickly and consistently.
concepts.body:
Both `type` and `interface` can name the shape of an object, and for plain objects they are nearly interchangeable:

```typescript
interface Point { x: number; y: number }
type PointT = { x: number; y: number };
```

The real differences:

- **Only `type` can name non-object types**: unions (`type Id = string | number`), literal types, tuples, function types, and the computed types of the Advanced lessons.
- **Only `interface` can be reopened**: two `interface Window { ... }` declarations combine into one (**declaration merging**). That's how packages let you add properties to their types (a later lesson). Declaring a `type` twice is an error.
- **Extending**: interfaces use `extends`; aliases combine with an **intersection type** `A & B`, which means "has everything from both". If the two conflict, `extends` reports an error at the declaration, while `&` silently produces an impossible property type such as `string & number` (that is, `never`) that you only discover later.
- **Performance and messages**: the compiler caches interface relationships by name and shows interface names in errors and hovers, while big intersections can be slower to check and print as long expanded types.

A common, defensible convention: use `interface` for object shapes (especially public, extendable ones) and `type` for everything else — unions, tuples, functions, and computed types. Another equally valid one is "`type` everywhere unless you need merging". Pick one per codebase and let a **linter** — a tool that flags risky or inconsistent code — enforce it (the typescript-eslint rule `consistent-type-definitions`).

A class can `implements` either form, as long as the alias describes an object type.
takeaways: `type` names any type; `interface` only object shapes
Interfaces merge and extend; aliases combine with `&`
Conflicting intersections quietly become `never`
Pick a convention and enforce it with a linter rule
pitfalls: Building large models out of many `&` intersections, which gives worse errors and slower checks than `extends`.

quiz.q: You need a name for "a string or an array of strings". Which is possible?
quiz.explain: Interfaces describe object shapes only; unions require a type alias.

quiz.q: Why can a library's users add properties to an interface the library exports, but not to an exported type alias?
options: Type aliases are erased and interfaces are not
quiz.explain: Redeclaring an interface merges members into it, whereas a type alias can be declared only once.

concepts.name: Optional and readonly properties
concepts.summary: Use readonly to prevent reassignment, understand what optional really means, and know the limits of both.
concepts.why: These modifiers document intent and catch accidental mutation, but they behave differently from what many people assume.
concepts.body:
**`readonly`** on a property forbids assigning to it after creation:

```typescript
interface Order { readonly id: string; total: number }
order.id = "x"; // error
```

It is a compile-time check only — nothing is frozen at runtime — and it is **shallow**: `readonly items: string[]` stops you replacing the array but not calling `items.push()`. Use `readonly string[]` for the array itself, or `Object.freeze` when you need runtime protection. Also, readonly is not enforced through another variable: a `{ readonly id: string }` value can be assigned to a variable typed `{ id: string }`, which can then change it.

**Optional** properties (`email?: string`) may be absent. When you read one, its type is `string | undefined`, so you must handle the missing case. By default TypeScript also lets you *assign* `undefined` explicitly — `{ email: undefined }` — which isn't quite the same as the key being absent (`"email" in obj` differs). The `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` option makes the distinction strict if your code cares.

Optional vs `| undefined`: `email?: string` means callers may omit the key; `email: string | undefined` means they must write it, even if the value is undefined. The second is useful when you want every call site to make an explicit choice.

For function parameters, the same ideas apply: `readonly` arrays as inputs advertise that you won't mutate them, and optional parameters must come after required ones.

Built-in **utility types** (a later lesson) do these changes for every property at once: `Readonly<T>` and `Partial<T>` make every property readonly or optional, and `Required<T>` removes the `?`.
takeaways: `readonly` is compile-time only and shallow
Use `readonly T[]` to block mutation of the array itself
`p?: T` = key may be missing; `p: T | undefined` = key required
pitfalls: Believing `readonly` makes nested arrays or objects immutable.

quiz.q: interface S { readonly list: number[] }. Which statement compiles?
quiz.explain: readonly applies only to the list property itself, not to the array it points to.

quiz.q: How do email?: string and email: string | undefined differ for someone creating the object?
options: The second lets you omit the key
The first forbids undefined values entirely
The first lets you omit the key; the second requires the key
quiz.explain: The ? modifier makes the key optional, while a required property with | undefined must still be written.

concepts.name: Enums and const objects
concepts.summary: Compare TypeScript enums with union types and as const objects, and know why many teams avoid enums.
concepts.why: You will meet enums in existing code, and choosing the right replacement affects bundles, tooling and interop.
concepts.body:
An **enum** declares a set of named constants. It is one of the few TypeScript features that emits real JavaScript code instead of being erased:

```typescript
enum Direction { Up, Down }            // numeric: Up = 0, Down = 1
enum Level { Info = "info", Warn = "warn" } // string enum
```

Numeric enums create a two-way object (`Direction[0] === "Up"`) and are loosely typed — older TypeScript versions even let any number be assigned to a numeric enum. String enums are stricter but **nominal** — matched by name, not shape: a function taking `Level` refuses the plain string `"info"`, which is awkward when values come from JSON. `const enum` copies the values straight into the code that uses them, but breaks under tools that compile one file at a time (`isolatedModules`).

Because enums aren't plain JavaScript, they also don't work with type-stripping runtimes (Node's built-in TypeScript support) and are disallowed by the `erasableSyntaxOnly` option. Many teams therefore prefer two alternatives:

- **A union of literal strings**: `type Level = "info" | "warn"`. No runtime footprint, plain strings everywhere, great autocomplete. Ideal when you don't need to iterate the values.
- **An `as const` object** plus a derived type, when you need the values at runtime too (for a dropdown, for checking input, for looping over them):

```typescript
const Level = { Info: "info", Warn: "warn" } as const;
type Level = (typeof Level)[keyof typeof Level]; // "info" | "warn"
```

`as const` makes the properties readonly literal types, `typeof` gets the object's type, and the indexed access (`[...]`, Advanced lesson) collects the values into a union. Using the same name for the value and the type is legal and reads naturally: `Level.Info` at runtime, `Level` as a type.

Enums are still fine in codebases that use them consistently — just know their quirks.
takeaways: Enums emit runtime code; string enums are nominal
Prefer unions of literal types when you only need types
`as const` object + `(typeof X)[keyof typeof X]` when you need runtime values too
pitfalls: Using `const enum` with isolatedModules-based tools (esbuild, Babel, swc), where it can't be inlined safely.

quiz.q: Given const Size = { S: "s", L: "l" } as const, what is (typeof Size)[keyof typeof Size]?
quiz.explain: keyof gives the keys, and indexing the object type with them yields the union of value types.

quiz.q: Why can't Node's built-in type stripping run a file containing an enum?
options: Enums need runtime code generation, not just type erasure
quiz.explain: Type stripping only deletes type syntax; an enum must be transformed into a JavaScript object.

concepts.name: Type predicates and assertion functions
concepts.summary: Write your own narrowing functions with value is T and asserts value is T.
concepts.why: Reusable checks turn messy data-checking code into clean, typed functions you can call anywhere.
takeaways: `x is T` return types turn boolean functions into reusable narrowing
`asserts x is T` narrows by throwing on failure
The compiler trusts predicates; keep them small and correct
TS 5.5+ infers simple predicates such as `x => x !== undefined`
pitfalls: Writing a predicate that returns true for values that don't actually match the claimed type.

quiz.q: function isNum(x: unknown): x is number { return true; } compiles. What happens if you call it on a string?
options: A runtime TypeError from the predicate
The string is narrowed to number and misuse goes undetected
quiz.explain: TypeScript trusts the declared predicate and does not check the body's logic.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between x is T and asserts x is T?
options: The first narrows based on a boolean result; the second narrows everything after the call and must throw on failure
The second only works on classes
The first only works in if statements inside the same function
quiz.explain: A predicate narrows in the branch where it returned true, while an assertion narrows the rest of the scope after it returns.

concepts.name: Discriminated unions
concepts.summary: Model states and variants as a union of objects sharing a literal tag, and handle them exhaustively.
concepts.why: This is the single most useful modelling technique in TypeScript: it makes impossible states impossible to write.
concepts.body:
A **discriminated union** is a union of object types that all share a property — the **discriminant** or tag — whose type is a different literal in each member:

```typescript
type Result =
  | { status: "loading" }
  | { status: "error"; error: Error }
  | { status: "success"; data: string[] };
```

Checking the tag narrows the whole object: inside `if (r.status === "success")` TypeScript knows `r.data` exists, and `r.error` is not even accessible. A `switch` on the tag is the idiomatic way to handle every case, ideally with an exhaustiveness check in `default` (assign to `never`) so that adding a new variant breaks the build in every place that must handle it.

Why this beats a single "bag of optionals" like `{ loading: boolean; error?: Error; data?: string[] }`: that type permits nonsense states (loading *and* errored, with data) and forces every reader to guess which combinations are real. The union lists exactly the legal states and the data each one carries.

Tips:

- Use string literals for tags; `kind`, `type` and `status` are common names. Booleans work too (`ok: true` / `ok: false`).
- Destructuring the tag into a separate `const` before checking still narrows, as long as both are `const`.
- The same technique models messages, events, steps of a form and replies from a server.
- Data-checking libraries such as Zod can produce these unions from a description of the expected data.

A `Result`-style type for errors — `{ ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E }` — is a lightweight way to make failure explicit in function signatures.
takeaways: Give each variant a literal tag; checking the tag narrows the whole object
Add a `never` check in `default` to catch unhandled variants
Prefer unions of states over objects full of optional properties
pitfalls: Making the tag a plain `string` instead of a literal — then nothing narrows.

quiz.q: In type R = { ok: true; value: number } | { ok: false; error: string }, what can you access after if (!r.ok)?
quiz.explain: ok being false identifies the second member, so only error is available.

quiz.q: What does assigning the switch variable to a never-typed constant in default achieve?
options: It makes the compiler fail if a union member isn't handled
It speeds up the switch at runtime
It is required for switch on unions
quiz.explain: If a case is missing, the variable still has that member's type, which isn't assignable to never.

concepts.name: Classes in TypeScript
concepts.summary: Type class fields, use access modifiers, parameter properties, implements and abstract classes.
concepts.why: Classes are common in Node services, Angular and many libraries, and TypeScript adds important checks on top of JS classes.
concepts.body:
TypeScript classes are JavaScript classes plus declarations for their members.

**Fields** must be declared with a type. With `strictPropertyInitialization` (part of `strict`), each field must be initialised in its declaration or the constructor; `name!: string` (definite assignment) opts out when something else sets it.

**Access modifiers**:

- `public` (the default), `protected` (the class and subclasses), `private` (only the class).
- These are **compile-time only** — `private` fields are ordinary properties at runtime. For real runtime privacy use JavaScript's own `#field` private fields, which TypeScript fully supports.
- `readonly` prevents reassignment after the constructor.

**Parameter properties** declare and assign a field in one go: `constructor(private readonly repo: Repo) {}`. It's concise and very common in Angular and NestJS code, but it is TypeScript-only syntax that emits code, so `erasableSyntaxOnly` and Node's type stripping reject it.

**`implements`** checks that a class satisfies an interface. It doesn't change the class's type or provide any implementation — it's purely a check, and the methods' parameter types are not inferred from the interface.

**`abstract`** classes can't be created with `new` and may declare `abstract` methods that subclasses must implement. Use **`override`** on methods that replace a parent's method; with `noImplicitOverride` the compiler requires it, catching typos and renamed base methods.

Remember a class declaration creates both a **value** (the constructor) and a **type** (the instance shape). Because typing is structural, any object with the right members can be used as the class type — unless the class has `private` or `#` members, which make it effectively nominal (matched by name).
takeaways: Declare fields with types; strict mode requires them to be initialised
`private`/`protected` are compile-time; `#private` is enforced at runtime
`implements` only checks the class; it doesn't type its members for you
Use `override` (with `noImplicitOverride`) on overriding methods
pitfalls: Expecting `private` to hide data at runtime (JSON.stringify and plain property access still see it).

quiz.q: A class has private secret: string. What does JSON.stringify(instance) include?
options: The secret property, because private is only enforced by the compiler
quiz.explain: TypeScript's private is erased; the field is an ordinary property at runtime, unlike #secret.

quiz.q: class C implements I { handle(x) { } } where I declares handle(x: string): void. What type does x have in C (with noImplicitAny on)?
options: It's an error: x implicitly has type any
quiz.explain: implements only checks compatibility; it does not contextually type the class's method parameters.

concepts.name: Generics
concepts.summary: Write functions and types that work over many types while keeping the link between input and output types.
concepts.why: Generics are what make typed collections, promises and reusable helpers possible; almost every library uses them.
concepts.body:
Suppose you write `function first(items: any[]): any`. It works for any array, but the result is `any` — you've lost the information that a `string[]` yields a `string`. **Generics** fix this with a **type parameter**, a variable that stands for a type:

```typescript
function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined {
  return items[0];
}
const n = first([1, 2, 3]); // T inferred as number → n: number | undefined
```

You declare type parameters in angle brackets and use them in the signature. At each call the compiler **infers** `T` from the arguments; you can also pass it explicitly as a **type argument** — `first<string>([])` — which is handy when there's nothing to infer from.

Types can be generic too. You already use them: `Array<T>`, `Promise<T>`, `Map<K, V>`, `Set<T>`. Define your own with aliases, interfaces and classes:

```typescript
interface ApiResponse<T> { data: T; status: number }
type Pair<A, B = A> = [A, B];   // B defaults to A
```

Guidelines for good generic signatures:

- A type parameter should **relate** two or more things — an input to an output, or two inputs. If `T` appears only once, you probably don't need it; use `unknown` or a concrete type.
- Use as few type parameters as possible and let inference do the work; callers should rarely need to write `<...>`.
- Name them `T`, `K`, `V`, `E` for simple cases, or descriptive names (`TItem`) in complex signatures.

Generic arrow functions are written `const id = <T,>(x: T) => x;` — the trailing comma avoids a clash with JSX, the HTML-like tags React code writes inside `.tsx` files.
takeaways: A type parameter `<T>` links input types to output types
Type arguments are usually inferred; pass them explicitly only when needed
Interfaces, aliases and classes can be generic too
If a type parameter is used only once, you likely don't need it
pitfalls: Writing `function f<T>(x: T): void` where `T` relates nothing — `unknown` says the same thing more simply.

quiz.q: Given function wrap<T>(x: T): { value: T }, what is the type of wrap("hi").value?
quiz.explain: T is inferred from the argument. Because T is unconstrained and appears inside an object, the literal widens to string.

quiz.q: Which signature makes the best use of a type parameter?
quiz.explain: Only last uses T to connect the input to the output; the others gain nothing from being generic.

concepts.name: Generic constraints and defaults
concepts.summary: Restrict type parameters with extends, use keyof in constraints, and give type parameters defaults.
concepts.why: Constraints let generic code use properties of T safely; without them generics can do almost nothing.
concepts.body:
An unconstrained `T` could be anything, so inside the function you can't touch any of its properties. A **generic constraint** says what `T` must at least be:

```typescript
function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T): T {
  return a.length >= b.length ? a : b;
}
longest("abc", "de");   // T = string
longest([1, 2], [3]);   // T = number[]
longest(10, 20);        // error: number has no length
```

Note that the function returns `T`, not `{ length: number }` — callers keep their precise type. That's the advantage over simply typing the parameter as `{ length: number }`.

Constraints can refer to other type parameters. The classic case is a typed property getter:

```typescript
function prop<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] { return obj[key]; }
```

`keyof T` is the union of `T`'s property names, so `K` must be a real key, and `T[K]` is the type of that property (both operators are covered in depth later). `prop(user, "nmae")` is an error and `prop(user, "age")` returns `number`.

**Defaults** work like default parameters: `interface Box<T = string>` lets callers write `Box` alone. A default must satisfy the constraint if there is one: `<T extends object = {}>`.

A subtle point: a constraint is a *lower bound on knowledge*, not the type itself. Inside `function f<T extends string>(x: T)` you can't return `"hello"` as `T`, because `T` might be the narrower literal `"bye"`. When you find yourself needing `as T`, the signature usually needs rethinking.

When inference picks a type from the "wrong" argument, `NoInfer<T>` (TS 5.4) marks a position that should not be used for inference.
takeaways: `T extends X` lets you use X's members on T while keeping T precise
`K extends keyof T` + `T[K]` type property access safely
Defaults (`<T = string>`) make generics easier to use
`NoInfer<T>` stops a parameter from influencing inference
pitfalls: Returning a concrete value `as T` — the caller's T may be narrower than the constraint.

quiz.q: Why is function f<T extends { id: number }>(x: T): T better than function g(x: { id: number }): { id: number }?
options: f returns the caller's full type, not just { id: number }
g cannot accept objects with extra properties
quiz.explain: The type parameter preserves the argument's specific type through to the result.

quiz.q: prop(obj, key) is declared <T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]. For obj = { a: 1, b: "x" } and key "b", what is returned?
quiz.explain: K is inferred as the literal "b", and T["b"] is string.

concepts.name: Built-in utility types
concepts.summary: Derive new types from existing ones with Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType and friends.
concepts.why: Utility types keep related types in step from one source of truth instead of copy-pasting shapes.
concepts.body:
TypeScript ships generic **utility types** that transform other types. Learning a dozen of them removes most hand-written duplication.

Reshaping objects:

- `Partial<T>` — all properties optional (great for update requests, where only changed values are sent).
- `Required<T>` — remove all `?`.
- `Readonly<T>` — all properties readonly (shallow).
- `Pick<T, "a" | "b">` — keep only those keys.
- `Omit<T, "password">` — drop keys. Note `Omit` doesn't check that the keys exist; a typo silently omits nothing.
- `Record<K, V>` — an object with keys `K` and values `V`, e.g. `Record<"en" | "fr", string>` requires both keys.

Working with unions:

- `Exclude<U, X>` / `Extract<U, X>` — remove or keep union members assignable to `X`.
- `NonNullable<T>` — remove `null` and `undefined`.

Working with functions and promises:

- `ReturnType<typeof fn>` and `Parameters<typeof fn>` — the return type and parameter tuple of a function type. Note the `typeof`: utilities take types, not values.
- `Awaited<T>` — the value a promise resolves to, unwrapping nested promises.

Strings: `Uppercase`, `Lowercase`, `Capitalize`, `Uncapitalize` transform literal string types.

A typical approach: define one main type and derive the rest — `type NewUser = Omit<User, "id" | "createdAt">`, `type UserPatch = Partial<NewUser>`. When `User` changes, everything follows.

None of these are magic: they're written with mapped and conditional types in `lib.es5.d.ts`, which you'll learn to write yourself in the Advanced lessons. Hover over one in your editor to see its definition.
takeaways: Derive types from one source with Pick, Omit, Partial, Record
`Exclude`/`Extract`/`NonNullable` filter unions
`ReturnType<typeof f>`, `Parameters<typeof f>`, `Awaited<T>` read types off functions and promises
pitfalls: Writing `ReturnType<fn>` instead of `ReturnType<typeof fn>` — utilities take types, not values.

quiz.q: type T = Omit<{ a: string; b: number }, "c">. What happens?
options: Compile error: "c" is not a key
T is { a: string; b: number }
quiz.explain: Omit's key parameter is not constrained to keyof T, so omitting a missing key is silently a no-op.

quiz.q: Which type requires an object to have exactly the keys "en" and "de" with string values?
quiz.explain: Record with a literal union of keys requires every listed key.

concepts.name: Typing async code
concepts.summary: Type promises and async functions, handle errors from catch, and type fetched data honestly.
concepts.why: Most application code is asynchronous; getting promise types and caught errors right avoids silent unsafety.
concepts.body:
An `async` function always returns a `Promise`. Its declared return type is `Promise<T>`, and inside you `return` a plain `T`:

```typescript
async function getCount(): Promise<number> { return 42; }
const n = await getCount(); // number
```

`Promise<T>` is generic: `.then` callbacks receive `T`, `await` unwraps it, and `Promise.all([a, b])` returns a tuple of each result type. `Awaited<T>` is the type-level version of `await`, useful with `ReturnType` on async functions.

**Errors are untyped.** A promise's type says nothing about how it can fail, and with `strict` (`useUnknownInCatchVariables`) a `catch (e)` variable is `unknown`. Narrow it before use: `e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e)`. The `.catch(err => ...)` callback's parameter is typed `any` by TypeScript's built-in type definitions, so annotate it as `unknown` yourself.

**External data is a trust boundary.** `fetch(...).then(r => r.json())` resolves to `any`. Writing `const user: User = await res.json()` is accepted, but it's an unchecked claim. Type it as `unknown` and check it (by hand or with a data-checking library such as Zod), or at least centralise the cast in one well-named function so the risk is visible.

**Forgotten awaits** are a classic bug: `if (isAdmin(user))` where `isAdmin` is async is always truthy because a promise is an object. TypeScript flags some of these (a promise in a condition when the function is known to return one), and the typescript-eslint linter rules `no-floating-promises` and `no-misused-promises` catch the rest — enable them.

Use `void` for async functions that return nothing: `Promise<void>`.
takeaways: Async functions return `Promise<T>`; `await` unwraps to `T`
Caught errors are `unknown` — narrow before use
`res.json()` is `any`: type it `unknown` and validate
Turn on the linter rules for floating and misused promises
pitfalls: Annotating `await res.json()` as your model type and treating it as validated.

quiz.q: What is the type of await Promise.all([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.resolve("a")])?
quiz.explain: Promise.all on a tuple of promises produces a tuple of their awaited types.

quiz.q: With strict enabled, what is the type of e in try { ... } catch (e) { }?
quiz.explain: useUnknownInCatchVariables (part of strict) types catch variables as unknown.

concepts.name: Modules, type imports and .d.ts files
concepts.summary: How TypeScript resolves imports, how to import types, and where types for JavaScript packages come from.
concepts.why: Module configuration and missing types are the most common sources of confusing errors in real projects.
concepts.body:
Any file with a top-level `import` or `export` is a **module**; TypeScript uses JavaScript's standard `import`/`export` (**ES modules**). Types can be exported and imported just like values:

```typescript
// user.ts
export interface User { id: number }
// app.ts
import type { User } from "./user.js";
```

**`import type`** (or `import { type User }`) marks an import as type-only, guaranteeing it is erased. With `verbatimModuleSyntax` enabled — recommended for new projects — the compiler requires this marking and otherwise leaves your imports exactly as written, which keeps behaviour predictable under bundlers and type-stripping runtimes.

**Module resolution** — how an import is matched to a file — depends on `module`/`moduleResolution`. Under `nodenext`, relative imports in ESM need the runtime file extension: you write `./user.js` even though the source is `user.ts`, because that's the path Node will load. With `"bundler"` resolution, extensionless imports are fine. Package imports follow the `"exports"` and `"types"` settings in the package's `package.json`.

**Where types come from** for a package your project uses (a **dependency**):

- Packages written in TypeScript or shipping their own **`.d.ts`** files (declared via `"types"`/`"exports"` in package.json) just work.
- Otherwise, community types often exist on **DefinitelyTyped**: `npm i -D @types/lodash`.
- If nothing exists, declare a minimal module yourself in a `.d.ts` file: `declare module "legacy-lib" { export function run(): void; }`, or a bare `declare module "legacy-lib";` that types everything as `any`.

A **declaration file** (`.d.ts`) contains only types — no implementations. `tsc` can generate them from your code with `declaration: true`. Files under `node_modules/@types` are included automatically (configurable with `types`), and `skipLibCheck: true` skips checking all `.d.ts` files, which speeds builds considerably.
takeaways: Use `import type` for types; turn on `verbatimModuleSyntax`
Under `nodenext`, write `./file.js` in imports of `.ts` files
Types come from the package, `@types/*`, or your own `declare module`
`.d.ts` files contain declarations only
pitfalls: Writing `./user.ts` or `./user` in imports under nodenext resolution, then hitting runtime or resolution errors.

quiz.q: Under module/moduleResolution nodenext, how should src/app.ts import src/util.ts?
quiz.explain: Node resolves the emitted file, so the specifier uses the .js extension the output will have.

quiz.q: A JavaScript package has no bundled types. What's the usual first thing to try?
quiz.explain: Community-maintained declarations are often published under the @types scope.

concepts.name: Strict mode and key compiler checks
concepts.summary: What strict turns on, and the extra checks worth enabling: noUncheckedIndexedAccess, exactOptionalPropertyTypes and more.
concepts.why: The difference between leaky and trustworthy TypeScript is mostly configuration; these flags define what the checker catches.
concepts.body:
`"strict": true` is a bundle of options, and new strict checks added in later versions join it automatically. The main ones:

- `noImplicitAny` — unannotated parameters can't silently become `any`.
- `strictNullChecks` — `null`/`undefined` are separate types.
- `strictFunctionTypes` — a callback that only handles specific inputs can't be passed where any input may arrive (details in the variance lesson).
- `strictPropertyInitialization` — class properties must be given a starting value.
- `strictBindCallApply` — `call`, `apply` and `bind` are checked against the function's parameter types.
- `useUnknownInCatchVariables` — `catch (e)` gives `e: unknown`.
- `noImplicitThis` and `alwaysStrict`.

You can switch individual members off (`"strict": true, "strictPropertyInitialization": false`) while migrating.

Valuable checks **outside** `strict`:

- `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` — `arr[i]` and `record[key]` include `undefined`. Catches real out-of-range bugs; costs some `!` or checks in loops (prefer `for...of`).
- `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` — `p?: string` no longer accepts an explicit `undefined`.
- `noImplicitOverride` — require the `override` keyword on methods that replace a parent's method.
- `noImplicitReturns`, `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch` — control-flow sanity.
- `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature` — force `obj["key"]` for dynamic keys.

Project hygiene flags: `isolatedModules` (each file can be compiled alone, required by esbuild/swc/Babel), `verbatimModuleSyntax`, and `skipLibCheck`.

To migrate an existing codebase, enable `strict`, then suppress the remaining errors per line with `// @ts-expect-error` (which itself errors once the problem is fixed, unlike `// @ts-ignore`) and pay them down gradually. Tools like `typescript-strict-plugin` can enforce strictness file by file.
takeaways: Always start with `strict: true`
Add `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` for honest index reads
Prefer `@ts-expect-error` over `@ts-ignore` for temporary suppressions
Use `isolatedModules` when another tool compiles your files
pitfalls: Disabling `strict` entirely to make a migration compile instead of disabling single sub-flags.

quiz.q: Which flag makes arr[5] have type T | undefined?
quiz.explain: Only noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds undefined to index reads; it is not part of strict.

quiz.q: Why prefer // @ts-expect-error over // @ts-ignore?
options: It reports an error when the line no longer has an error, so stale suppressions are found
quiz.explain: An unused @ts-expect-error is itself an error, so fixed problems don't leave silent suppressions behind.

concepts.name: keyof, typeof and indexed access types
concepts.summary: Turn values into types with typeof, get property-name unions with keyof, and look up member types with T[K].
concepts.why: These three operators are the vocabulary for deriving types from other types and from real runtime values.
concepts.body:
Three operators let you compute types instead of writing them out.

**`typeof` in a type position** gives the type of a variable or property: `type Config = typeof defaultConfig`. It's the bridge from values to types — write the object once and derive its type. It only accepts identifiers and property accesses, not arbitrary expressions (`typeof f()` is invalid; use `ReturnType<typeof f>`).

**`keyof T`** is the union of `T`'s property names as literal types: `keyof { a: 1; b: 2 }` is `"a" | "b"`. Two surprises:

- For a type with a string index signature, `keyof` is `string | number`, because JavaScript converts numeric keys to strings.
- `keyof` of a union only gives keys present in *every* member.

**Indexed access types** `T[K]` look up the type of a property: `User["email"]` is `string`. `K` can be a union (`User["id" | "name"]` gives the union of those property types) and must be a valid key, otherwise it's an error. Two common idioms:

- `T[keyof T]` — the union of all property value types.
- `T[number]` — the element type of an array or tuple type, e.g. `(typeof roles)[number]`.

Combined they let a single runtime constant drive all its related types:

```typescript
const roles = ["admin", "editor", "viewer"] as const;
type Role = (typeof roles)[number]; // "admin" | "editor" | "viewer"
```

Note the parentheses — `typeof roles[number]` parses the same way, but writing them makes intent clear. Indexed access works on types, not values: `User["email"]` is valid in a type, while `const k = "email"; User[k]` is not — use `User[typeof k]`.

These operators are the inputs to mapped and conditional types, coming next.
takeaways: `typeof value` turns a runtime value into a type
`keyof T` = union of property names; `T[K]` = property type
`T[number]` gets an array/tuple's element type
Derive types from one constant instead of duplicating them
pitfalls: Writing `typeof someFunction()` — typeof only takes names; use `ReturnType<typeof someFunction>`.

quiz.q: What is keyof { [key: string]: number }?
quiz.explain: Numeric property keys are converted to strings in JavaScript, so a string index signature accepts both.

quiz.q: Given const sizes = ["s", "m"] as const, which type is "s" | "m"?
quiz.explain: Indexing the tuple's type with number gives the union of its element types; sizes[number] is invalid because sizes is a value.

concepts.name: Mapped types
concepts.summary: Build object types by iterating over keys with { [K in Keys]: ... }, adding or removing modifiers and remapping keys.
concepts.why: Mapped types let one declaration produce whole families of related types, and they're how Partial, Readonly and Record work.
concepts.body:
A **mapped type** creates an object type by looping over a union of keys:

```typescript
type Flags<T> = { [K in keyof T]: boolean };
```

For each key `K` in `keyof T`, the result has a property `K` of type `boolean`. The right-hand side can use `K` and `T[K]`, so you can transform each property's type: `{ [K in keyof T]: () => T[K] }` turns every property into a getter function.

**Modifiers** can be added or removed with `+` / `-`:

- `{ readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }` — this is `Readonly<T>`.
- `{ [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }` — `Partial<T>`.
- `{ -readonly [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }` — remove both, giving a mutable `Required`.

When you map over `keyof T` for a type parameter `T`, the mapped type is **homomorphic**: it preserves the original optional and readonly modifiers, and it maps arrays and tuples to arrays and tuples instead of to objects with numeric keys.

**Key remapping** with `as` changes or filters the keys:

```typescript
type Getters<T> = { [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K] };
type OnlyStrings<T> = { [K in keyof T as T[K] extends string ? K : never]: T[K] };
```

Mapping a key to `never` drops it — that's how you filter properties by their value type. (`string & K` is needed because keys may also be numbers or symbols, which `Capitalize` can't take.)

You can also map over any union, not just `keyof`: `{ [L in "en" | "fr"]: string }` is essentially `Record<"en" | "fr", string>`.

Mapped types read best when named and kept small; compose several simple ones rather than writing one giant expression.
takeaways: `{ [K in keyof T]: ... }` transforms every property of T
`+`/`-` add or remove `readonly` and `?`
`as` remaps keys; mapping a key to `never` removes it
Homomorphic maps keep modifiers and array/tuple shapes
pitfalls: Forgetting `string & K` when building template-literal keys, since keys can also be number or symbol.

quiz.q: What does type M<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] } do to { a?: number }?
options: Makes a required, with type number
quiz.explain: -? strips the optional modifier; for a homomorphic mapped type the undefined that came from ? is removed too.

quiz.q: How do you drop properties from a mapped type?
options: Remap their key to never with as
Use Exclude on the result object
quiz.explain: A key remapped to never is omitted from the result; a never value would keep the key.

concepts.name: Conditional types and infer
concepts.summary: Choose types with T extends U ? X : Y, understand distribution over unions, and extract parts of types with infer.
concepts.why: Conditional types power ReturnType, Awaited and most advanced library typings; you need them to read and write those.
concepts.body:
A **conditional type** picks one of two types based on whether one type fits — is **assignable** to — another:

```typescript
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;
```

It's a type-level ternary. Its power comes from two features.

**Distribution.** When the checked type is a *naked* type parameter (on its own, not wrapped in anything) and you fill it in with a union, the condition is applied to each member separately and the results are unioned. That's how `Exclude` works:

```typescript
type Exclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T;
// Exclude<"a" | "b" | "c", "a">  →  "b" | "c"
```

Usually that's what you want, but not always. Wrap both sides in a tuple — `[T] extends [U] ? ...` — to treat the union as a whole. Also note that `never` is the empty union, so a distributive conditional over `never` yields `never` — a common source of puzzling results.

**`infer`.** Inside the `extends` clause you can declare a type variable to capture part of the matched type:

```typescript
type ElementOf<T> = T extends readonly (infer E)[] ? E : never;
type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : T;
```
